newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Bills unpaid, lights go out on Ferdinand Marcos.
newsitem.headline: Bills unpaid, lights go out on Ferdinand Marcos.

text.p: The lights went out on former president Ferdinand Marcos on Monday after a Philippine power firm cut the electricity to a mausoleum where his corpse is lying in a glass coffin.
"This is the ultimate harassment, the harassment of the dead, the dead who cannot speak up to defend himself," former first lady Imelda Marcos told reporters in Manila.

Workers of the Ilocos Norte Electric Cooperative pulled the plug on the family compound in the northern Philippine town of Batac, Marcos's home town, after the family failed to pay bills totalling 5.643 million pesos ($214,500), cooperative officials said.

The corpse of the man who ruled the Philippines for 20 years until he was overthrown in a "people revolt" in 1986 has lain in an elevated glass coffin in the air-conditioned crypt since its return to the country in 1993.
Preserved by chemical injections, the cadaver had been lit by soft, eerie lights 24 hours a day and surrounded by the strains of classical music in the background.

Marcos died in exile in Hawaii in 1989 but it was not until four years later when his cousin, Fidel Ramos, took over the presidency that the government allowed his remains to be brought into the country.
Marcos's successor, Corazon Aquino, had barred the cadaver from the country, fearing its presence might spark violence among the supporters of the former ruler.
Imelda Marcos, now a congresswoman, added: "This is the ultimate oppression, the opression of someone who is dead."
Officials of the cooperative said they had given the family until the close of business last Friday to pay the bills but by Monday morning no one had settled them.
Officials earlier said the family was questioning the bills, which includes unpaid demands over several years.

"We waited for word from the Marcoses and gave them time to settle the account but it seems nobody would like to negotiate, so we cut it off," Eduardo Arzadon, a department manager of the cooperative, told Reuters.
Mrs Marcos did not say how the family would settle the bills but suggested it might be time for the government to allow Marcos to be buried in Manila, as the family had always wished.
Ramos had refused a burial in the capital, fearing it might provoke unrest.
"Maybe with this development, Ferdinand could finally be buried here (in Manila)," she said.
Marcos's embalmer Frank Malabed said in Manila that with air-conditioning, the preserved body could last until 2000 without fresh injections of chemicals.

If the power was off for only a couple of months, the corpse would not be affected, "but if it lasts for many months, it can develop mould and then we will have to go and check to see if its internal parts are being affected", he said.
